A
Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
Sir Gawain and the Green Knightis a \ong poem, one of four written in the dialect of the
North-west Midlands of England, which are contained in a fourteenth century manuscript.
This manuscript is the sole source of Gawain. The plot is made up of two originally separate
stories — the ‘Beheading Test’ and the ‘Temptation’ — the first of which can be traced back to
the eighth-century Irish saga, Bricriu’s Feast. Although Gawain begins at the court of King
Arthur, where Sir Gawain is one of his Knights of the Round Table, neither Beheading nor
Temptation had anything to do with the Arthurian legends originally.
The Gawain poet must be credited with structural ability of a high order in fusing together
diverse elements. The poem is a masterful combination of two entirely unconnected
adventures, so managed as to produce a harmonious unit. No reader who was unaware of
its origins would suspect that it had been put together out of elements that originally had
nothing to do with each other.
In the manuscript the poem is divided by large capital letters into four sections which are, in
effect, the main stages in the development of the story. In the first, the time is New Year’s
Day, the place is King Arthur's court. A mysterious warrior who is completely green, from his
clothes and hair to his beard and skin, enters and offers to allow anyone to strike him with
his axe if the challenger will take a return blow in a year and a day. Gawain accepts, and
beheads him in one blow, only to have the Green Knight stand up, pick up his head, and
remind Gawain to meet him at the Green Chapel at the appointed time. The second section
describes Gawain’s winter journey in search of the Green Chapel and his arrival on Christmas
Eve at a castle, where he is warmly welcomed by the lord and lady. The lord persuades him
to stay as his quest until New Year’s Day, when he promises to have him escorted to the
Green Chapel. Further, Gawain accepts the lord’s merry proposal that the last three days of
the old year shall be enlivened by an agreement to exchange anything they happen to win
on each of these three days. In the third section Gawain’s search for the Green Chapel is
subordinated for the time being to three temptations. On the first two days Gawain faithfully
exchanges the lady’s kisses for the spoils of the lord’s hunting expeditions; on the third day,
however, he conceals from the lord the green belt that the lady has given him. The fourth
section describes how Gawain is conducted to the Green Chapel, how the Green Knight aims
three blows at him and wounds him slightly with the third blow. He explains to Gawain the
significance of the two pretended blows and of the slight wound he has inflicted with his
third blow. The mortified Gawain then returns to Arthur's court.
There is a considerable amount of suspense in the poem. The text between the first and
second sections bridges the gap between New Year's Day and All Saints’ Day (1st
November), when Gawain sets out on his quest for the Green Chapel; but they are also
tinged with melancholy and foreboding, and help to create suspense by putting a gloomy
question mark after future events. During the whole of the third section we are kept
guessing about the relationship between the Beheading and the Temptation. It is not until
the fourth section, when the Green Knight reveals himself as Bertilak, the lord of the castle,
that we are in a position to understand the significance of some of the details of the third
section — why, for instance, the lady knew about Gawain’s dangerous mission, and why she
chose to describe the green belt as a charm against violent death in order to persuade
Gawain to accept it.

E The poem’s internal unity springs from its central theme of the testing of Gawain: the
outcome of the Beheading depends upon the outcome of the Temptation, and this in turn
depends upon Gawain himself. The poet tells his story in such a way that Gawain’s
successful fulfilment of his mission is never a foregone conclusion. Above all, the poet is
careful to make Gawain very human, in spite of his many virtues. And his actions, simply
because he is so human, cannot be precisely calculated in advance. And yet the proof of
Gawain’s humanity is not limited to one or two major lapses from his high ideals of conduct;
it rather consists of innumerable small touches which, all together, give him full membership
of the society of ordinary mortals. As a result of his quest Gawain is spiritually reborn, in a
Parallel to the underlying seasonal myth of death and revival.
